summary.prose: When a repository is added, the daemon now sets its build commands itself: for a Python, Go, Rust or JVM project it stores that type's typical typecheck and test commands (and the exit-code result format) in the repo's own settings, once, without asking anyone and without overwriting anything already set. A Node project keeps the gate's own default and a project of an unknown type gets nothing. The result of the add says what was done. The Repo Configuration page of each client gets its own Build section to see and edit the three commands, and for a repo that has none (added before this change, or of an unknown type) it shows the type's typical commands as suggestions to apply.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Standalone feature — no parent HLD. Design directly against the repo, grounded on the s1 analyze passes. There are no HLD shared contracts to honour.

boundary.internal: Set the build commands when a repo is added and edit them on the Repo Configuration page

api.name: repo.add
api.signature: 'repo.add': (params: { path: string; steering?: SteeringSelection }) => Promise<{ ok: true; steering?: SteeringResult; mcp?: McpResult; buildDefaults?: BuildDefaultsOutcome }>

parameters.name: path
parameters.purpose: The repository path to register, validated as before.

parameters.name: steering
parameters.purpose: As before: the steering-block and MCP selection; unrelated to the build defaults.

returns.meaning: As before, plus buildDefaults: what the build-defaults follow-up did.

errors.condition: The path is invalid, as before; the build defaults never add an error.

postconditions: The repo is registered and indexing has started whatever the build defaults did.
No build setting is written for a Node or unknown project, nor when the repo's entry already sets typecheckCommand, testCommand or resultFormat.
buildDefaults is always present once the registration succeeded.

api.name: applyBuildDefaults
api.signature: function applyBuildDefaults(repoPath: string, deps?: { readonly writeKeys?: typeof writeRepoEntryKeys; readonly configPath?: () => string }): Promise<BuildDefaultsOutcome>

parameters.name: deps
parameters.purpose: The injectable writer and file path the repo settings handlers already take.

returns.meaning: Whether the defaults were written, for which project type and which commands, or why nothing was written.

postconditions: Never throws: a failed read or write is reported as reason 'write-failed' with the message.
Writes the three keys in one call of the serialised writer (typecheckCommand, testCommand, resultFormat 'exit-code'), so a lone command is never stored.
Reads the repo's own entry first and writes nothing when any of the three keys is present.

api.name: repo.settings.get
api.signature: 'repo.settings.get': (params: { repo: string }) => Promise<SettingsResult>   // SettingsResult.payload: RepoSettingsPayload gains buildSetup

parameters.name: repo
parameters.purpose: The registered repository's exact path, as before.

returns.meaning: As before, plus payload.buildSetup: the project type, where the gate's commands come from and, for a repo with no commands and a type that has typical commands, the suggestion.

errors.condition: The path is not a registered repository, as before.

postconditions: Nothing is written: buildSetup is derived from the repo root's marker files and the repo's own entry.
buildSetup.suggestion is present only when commandsSource is 'none' and the project type is python, go, rust or jvm.
A repo whose entry holds an invalid build setting reports commandsSource 'invalid' with a note, and no suggestion.

api.name: buildSettingsRows
api.signature: function buildSettingsRows(fields: readonly RepoFieldDef[], payload: RepoSettingsPayload): SettingsRow[]

parameters.name: payload
parameters.purpose: The repo's settings payload, now carrying buildSetup.

returns.meaning: The terminal's rows; an unset Build row shows its suggestion as the placeholder.

postconditions: Rows keep the daemon's order and labels; only the placeholder of an unset Build row changes.

api.name: renderRepoConfig

returns.meaning: The VS Code Repo Configuration page, whose Build rows move from a sub-heading of the Tracker grid into a section of their own.

postconditions: The Build rows keep their keys, labels and kinds; the shared repo-fields contract still holds.

dataModelChanges.details: { applied: boolean; projectType: 'node' | 'python' | 'go' | 'rust' | 'jvm' | 'unknown'; typecheckCommand?: string; testCommand?: string; resultFormat?: 'exit-code'; reason?: 'already-set' | 'node-default' | 'no-typical-commands' | 'write-failed'; note?: string }. Returned by repo.add as buildDefaults; never stored.
Adds the optional-by-version field buildDefaults to the { ok, steering?, mcp? } result; a client that ignores it behaves as before.
Adds `buildSetup: BuildSetup`, always present, read-only (not a settings row).

{ projectType: 'node' | 'python' | 'go' | 'rust' | 'jvm' | 'unknown'; commandsSource: 'node-default' | 'repo-setting' | 'none' | 'invalid'; note?: string; suggestion?: { typecheckCommand: string; testCommand: string; resultFormat: 'exit-code' } }. Derived on each read and never stored.

The rows (typecheckCommand, testCommand, resultFormat) are unchanged; how a client groups them changes: the VS Code page renders them in a section of their own, and the shared fixture src/config/__tests__/fixtures/repo-fields-catalog.json gains the buildSetup of its repo.settings.get payload.

errorCases.scenario: The defaults cannot be written at repo add (github.json changed by another process on each attempt, or the write fails)
errorCases.detection: writeRepoEntryKeys returns { ok: false, error: { code: 'file-changed' | 'write-failed' } } inside applyBuildDefaults
errorCases.response: applyBuildDefaults returns { applied: false, reason: 'write-failed', note } and logs it; the repo is registered and indexed regardless; nothing is stored, so no lone command is left
errorCases.userImpact: The repo reads 'the gate ran nothing' until its commands are set; the Build section shows the project type's typical commands as suggestions to apply

errorCases.scenario: The repo's own entry cannot be read before the write (github.json unreadable or malformed)
errorCases.detection: readRepoEntry returns { ok: false, error: { code: 'github-json-unreadable' } }
errorCases.response: Nothing is written (the entry's contents are unknown, so an existing value could be overwritten); the outcome is { applied: false, reason: 'write-failed', note } and the add succeeds
errorCases.userImpact: The add succeeds; the settings file is reported unreadable on the Repo Configuration page as it is today

errorCases.scenario: The stored default is wrong for the project (it uses ruff instead of mypy, a task runner instead of go test) or its tool is not installed
errorCases.detection: The build gate runs the stored command and gets a non-zero exit code, a failing report or a 'could not start' note, which its verdict and the test record show
errorCases.response: The gate fails the check with that command's own output, as it would for any stored setting; the user edits the three commands on the Build section, and a later repo add never overwrites the edit
errorCases.userImpact: A build fails with the command's output, which names the command, until the user corrects it; the default was a guess the user accepted by choosing automatic defaults

errorCases.scenario: A client is older or newer than the daemon and the repo.add result or the settings payload lacks buildDefaults or buildSetup
errorCases.detection: The field is undefined when the client reads it
errorCases.response: The client shows nothing about the defaults and no suggestion, and renders the Build rows as before
errorCases.userImpact: Same as today; the daemon still wrote the defaults, which the user sees on the page

edgeCases.expected: The type's PROJECT_TYPE_GUIDANCE typecheck and test commands and resultFormat 'exit-code' are written together, and the outcome is { applied: true, ... } with the commands

edgeCases.input: The entry sets only one of the three keys, for example resultFormat

edgeCases.expected: The root decides the type (node): nothing is written

invariantsToPreserve.text: repo.add keeps registering the repo and starting indexing exactly as before; its follow-ups stay guarded so that a failure is logged and never fails the add, and the build defaults follow the same contract

The daemon stays the only writer of github.json, through the serialised writeRepoEntryKeys; the defaults are written as ordinary settings that repo.settings.set can change or clear, and repo.settings.set keeps its validation and registered-repo rule
A value already set in the repo's own entry is never overwritten by the defaults

The typical commands come only from PROJECT_TYPE_GUIDANCE in the daemon, and the gate runs a command only from the Node default or a stored repo setting; it refuses a lone command, so the three keys are written together
Every client renders the same key, label, kind and note per repoFields row, in the daemon's order, from the shared fixture; the new section changes no row

migration.stateBefore: repo.add registers a repository, starts indexing and runs the steering and MCP follow-ups only when asked, each guarded so a failure never fails the add; no path writes a build setting at add, and the add is mostly non-interactive (the search.text bundle). A repo's build commands are keys of its own entry in github.json written only through repo.settings.set or by hand, rendered by the three clients with no project-type suggestion (the module.profile bundle). The typical commands of each project type exist only in PROJECT_TYPE_GUIDANCE and feed the builder prompts; the gate runs a command only from the Node default or a stored setting (the usage.example bundle). A non-Node repo therefore reads 'the gate ran nothing' until its commands are set by hand.
migration.stateAfter: repo.add also calls a guarded applyBuildDefaults after the registration: for a Python, Go, Rust or JVM repo whose entry sets none of the three build keys it stores that type's typecheck and test commands and resultFormat exit-code in one write, and the result reports what happened (buildDefaults). Node and unknown repos and repos whose entry already sets a key are left as they are. The defaults are ordinary settings, editable or clearable afterwards. repo.settings.get also returns a read-only buildSetup (type, commands source, suggestion for a repo with none), and each client's Repo Configuration page shows the Build rows as a section of their own with the suggestion as the placeholder of an unset row.

migrationSteps.action: Add buildSetupFor and applyBuildDefaults in the daemon's repo settings module; return buildSetup from repo.settings.get; nothing calls applyBuildDefaults yet and no stored data changes
Call applyBuildDefaults from repo.add as a guarded follow-up and return buildDefaults in the result; this is the first write at add, for repos added from then on
Regenerate the shared repoFields fixture's repo.settings.get payload with a buildSetup, and teach the terminal rows model to show the suggestion as the placeholder of an unset Build row
Terminal and VS Code: give the Repo Configuration screen and page a Build section of their own
JetBrains: give the repo settings a Build section of their own; its Kotlin tests are run by the user
Document the automatic defaults and the Build section in docs/daemon.md

migration.backwardCompat: No existing method changes shape: repo.add gains an optional result field and repo.settings.get one field, which an older client ignores, and a newer client facing an older daemon finds them absent and shows nothing extra. No stored data is rewritten: only repos added after the change get defaults, and repos already registered keep exactly what they have (their page offers the suggestion). Rolling the code back leaves the stored commands in place; they are ordinary settings the gate keeps honouring. repo.settings.set, the repoFields rows and their order are unchanged.

alternativesConsidered.name: The daemon writes the type's default commands in repo.add, once, when none are set
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: After registration, repo.add detects the project type and stores its typical commands in the repo's own entry unless the entry already sets a build key; the Build section edits them afterwards.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add a small daemon function applyBuildDefaults(repoPath) that reads the repo's own entry with readRepoEntry, returns without writing when typecheckCommand, testCommand or resultFormat is already set or when the project type is node (the gate's own default) or unknown (its guidance is prose), and otherwise writes the type's PROJECT_TYPE_GUIDANCE typecheck and test command and resultFormat 'exit-code' with the existing serialised writer writeRepoEntryKeys. The repo.add handler calls it after the registration as a guarded follow-up, like the steering and MCP follow-ups: a failure is logged and never fails the add, and the result gains buildDefaults (applied, project type, commands, or the reason nothing was written). No client prompts. The Repo Configuration page of each client renders the Build rows as a section of their own; for a repo with no commands (added before this change, or of an unknown type) repo.settings.get returns a read-only buildSetup whose suggestion the page shows as the placeholder with a 'use suggested' action.
pros: Works for every way of adding a repo (terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, scripts) with no client change at add and no user intervention.
Reuses the existing writer, the existing validation and the one command table in the daemon; the stored value is an ordinary setting, visible and editable on the Build section.
Never overwrites a value the user set, and never makes the add fail.
cons: The default is a guess from marker files (a Python project may use ruff, a Go project a task runner); a wrong default makes the gate fail with that command's output instead of saying it ran nothing, until the user edits it.
A new write in repo.add, a handler that so far wrote nothing in the repo's settings.

alternativesConsidered.name: The gate uses the type's typical commands when no setting exists, nothing stored
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: commandProfileOf falls back to PROJECT_TYPE_GUIDANCE for python, go, rust and jvm; no write at add.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Change commandProfileOf so a project of those types with no repo setting gets commandsSource 'type-default' and the table's commands instead of 'none'; nothing is written at repo add; the Build section shows the effective default as a read-only placeholder and an edit stores a setting that wins.
pros: Smallest write surface: no write in repo.add, and existing repos are covered at once.
No file to keep in step with the table when the table changes.
cons: The gate would run commands the user can neither see stored nor has set, and the repo's settings say nothing is set while builds run something.
Reverses the invariant from the build-gate Story that the gate runs a command only from the Node default or a repo setting, and the prompts and 'the gate ran nothing' wording that rest on it.
Does not 'set the commands when the repo is added': nothing is set.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: The gate would run commands that are stored nowhere, so the settings and the behaviour disagree, and the build-gate Story's invariant that the gate runs only the Node default or a stored setting would have to be reversed.

alternativesConsidered.name: Each client writes the defaults after the add with repo.settings.set, without asking
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: After repo.add succeeds, the terminal, VS Code and JetBrains clients read buildSetup and write the suggestion at once.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Keep the buildSetup block of repo.settings.get with its suggestion and have each client, right after a successful add, write the suggestion through repo.settings.set with no prompt.
pros: The daemon's repo.add stays as it is.
The write uses the existing set path and its validation.
cons: Three clients each implement the same silent write, and the repo.add of any other caller (a script, the CLI's non-interactive add) sets nothing.
Two writes with a failure window between them (the lone-command case the gate refuses), repeated in every client.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: The same silent write would be duplicated in three clients, and the non-interactive callers that matter most (a script's repo.add) would set nothing.

alternativesConsidered.name: A Build section on the Repo Configuration pages only, no default at add
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Each client gets its own Build section with the type's suggestion as the placeholder; the user sets the commands from the page.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Render the Build rows as a section of their own on the terminal screen, the VS Code page and the JetBrains settings, with the suggestion from repo.settings.get as the placeholder and a 'use suggested' action. repo.add is unchanged.
pros: The smallest change, and nothing is written that the user did not choose.
cons: Does not meet the request: the commands are not set when the repo is added, so a non-Node repo's builds read 'the gate ran nothing' until the user finds the page.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: It leaves the commands unset at add, which is what the request asks to change.
